Mourir entre les mailles du système: Dying Through the Cracks of the System
« Il faut continuer, ne pas s’arrêter, a: “We have to keep going, not stop, help. That’s the goal.”
Manon Fleurant, ancienne locataire de la: Manon Fleurant, former tenant of the Société d'habitation populaire de l'Est de Montréal (SHAPEM). Photo: Christelle Saint-Julien
« J’ai sauvé des vies », dit sans détour: “I saved lives,” Manon Fleurant says flatly. For two years, she lived on Pelletier Street, in a unit owned by the Société d’habitation populaire de l’Est de Montréal (SHAPEM), a nonprofit housing organization. Six months ago, she left Montréal-Nord and moved into a public housing unit (HLM) in the Mercier–Hochelaga-Maisonneuve borough. “Otherwise, I’d still be there,” she adds. Today, Manon is back at her old home to run the monthly food distribution for residents, an initiative she set up herself. For the occasion, she asked her sister and a friend to come lend a hand. “I still take care of the kitchen, it lets me keep in touch. It lets them see me, and me see them – they weren’t happy when I left,” says Manon.
On comprend rapidement pourquoi : Manon: It’s easy to see why: Manon invests herself enormously in her neighbours, to the point of becoming a lifeline. Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, she handled the food distribution. At first she did it from her own place, on the third floor, passing the food down with a rope. When it became possible, she and her fellow volunteers moved into the community space made available to them by Paroles D’Exclues, a nonprofit driven by citizen mobilization and research, whose offices are on SHAPEM’s property. “Some of them would have died in their apartments,” says the former resident. During their regular visits to distribute food, Manon Fleurant and Daniel Bissonnette, also a resident, noticed the health conditions and needs of several people. Manon describes how she called 911 for a neighbour, Fred*, without his knowledge. “The doctor said that a few more days and he would have been dead,” she says of the man, who spent several months in hospital. Today, he is doing well.
D’autres ont eu moins de chance. Dès son: Others were less fortunate. As soon as she arrived, Manon became friends with Célia. “The doctor said, ‘I’ve never seen anyone smile until their last breath,’” she recounts of her friend, whose good mood was contagious. Manon explains that the woman, who was in her sixties and lived alone, suffered from Lou Gehrig’s disease, diagnosed too late. “Nobody listened to me,” she says with regret. She could see her friend’s health deteriorating rapidly during the pandemic. “Name it, I called the CLSC, social services... We weren’t heard, until the last time, but by the last time, it was too late.” Manon says she called an ambulance for her friend several times. Once, the emergency crew left without her. The next time, she was discharged from hospital the following day. “I called her sister, I told her, ‘My God, she’s going to stay in her apartment, something has to be done,’” she recalls. She convinced the patient to go back to the hospital, and Célia left in an ambulance again. “When the doctor saw her, he said she wouldn’t be coming out,” Manon says sadly. Célia never came home; she died a month later. “Because nobody listened to me,” she repeats. “They could have done something well before that to ease her suffering.”
Quelques mois plus tôt, Marcel*, un vois: A few months earlier, Marcel*, a neighbour, died alone at home. “He’d come by, he’d always stop,” says Manon, who saw him every day when he went to the corner store. He was well known and involved with SHAPEM’s residents, and often busied himself cleaning the yard and the surrounding area. “We often gave Marcel food, and he’d bring some back for his neighbours,” says Manon, speaking to his generosity.
Et puis, elle ne l’a plus revu. Ses appe: And then she stopped seeing him. Her calls went unanswered, and she went several days without news. “If he had health problems, he didn’t talk about them, he never complained, he was always happy to see us,” says Manon of her neighbour, who drank heavily. Residents alerted the staff of Paroles D’Exclues. An employee went to check and saw Marcel on the floor of his apartment, where his death was confirmed. A little less than a month ago, Elzéar* was found dead. Manon and Daniel believe they were the last to hear from him, at last month’s food distribution. Two weeks later, someone called Manon to tell her he had died at home. “He had mobility problems, I know he was very sick, I don’t know what he had. That’s another one we lost,” Manon laments. “They’re good people,” Manon says of those who are gone. “Despite their health or their problems.”
« Ce n’est pas l’fun, être seul ; person: “It’s no fun being alone; nobody in life wants to be alone,” says Daniel Bissonnette, an engaged resident. “Some people do it by choice, but often it’s a combination of circumstances,” he believes. He has lived in SHAPEM housing for nearly 12 years.
Daniel Bissonnette, locataire de la Soci: Daniel Bissonnette, tenant of the Société d'habitation populaire de l'Est de Montréal (SHAPEM). Photo: Julien Forest
Daniel estime à 200 le nombre de logemen: Daniel estimates that there are 200 units in the Habitations de la SHAPEM on Pelletier Street. Families live there, but a majority of residents are people living alone, often aged 50 and over. In total, SHAPEM manages a housing stock of 1,750 units.
Au Québec, 1,2 million de personnes vive: In Quebec, 1.2 million people live alone, according to Statistics Canada’s 2016 census figures. That is 17% of the population, a proportion that has doubled over the past 30 years. In Montréal, the figure reached 21% of the population, compared with 28% of households nationwide, or 4 million Canadians. These surveys noted that people living alone were in poorer mental and physical health than those living with others. Today, alongside his partner in crime Manon, Daniel makes sandwiches with an expert hand. When his former neighbour isn’t there, he continues his work on other citizen projects dedicated to residents. “Knowing there are people around who notice if you haven’t been seen is reassuring,” says Daniel. “When you live alone, especially if you don’t go out much, you’d better hope someone is keeping an eye on you.” He mentions a neighbour who is struggling and sick. He’ll drop by later. “With the food bank, we were able to see that people weren’t doing well.
On a mis tellement de choses de l’avant: We put so many things forward during the pandemic,” he says. He also tells the story of Célia*. He has plenty of other stories. Lives saved, others lost. “It happens regularly that someone is found,” he says regretfully. He describes how, since the pandemic, community organizations have been absent from the premises. “No activities were put forward, except those by the residents,” he says. Reopening didn’t bring those services back on site. “All the access we had before closed, despite the reopening,” Daniel continues. He points out that residents live in a service desert. There is no clinic or pharmacy nearby, and the closest supermarket is in Laval, on the other side of the bridge.
Il dénonce le fait qu’il est difficile d: He condemns how hard it is to get help from the health and social services, which are supposed to be there for exactly that. “It’s a government bureaucratic machine. You can have problems today, call the CLSC, and you won’t get service tomorrow morning. CLSCs are so bureaucratized that nothing works anymore,” the resident laments. Daniel also observes that few measures actually reach people where they are. “You have to work on the ground. That’s where reality happens.”
Il souligne les efforts et les initiativ: He highlights the efforts and initiatives of the Habitations de la SHAPEM residents during the pandemic, which the local CLSC staff were invited to see at a meeting. The event left a strong impression on him. “We managed to get them out of their offices. It was a great day,” he remembers. Daniel says their guests themselves were happy to get out, and had to explain to their bosses why they were going there. “Getting them out of their offices was the deal of the century. Yet it’s outside their offices that things happen,” he argues. He hopes the visit showed how useful community-based services can be. “If we don’t show innovation and imagination, and if we don’t care about one another, nothing will happen.” For 25 years, Daniel worked as an orderly. He is critical of the health care system, in particular its lack of access. “The emergency room is the front door of the health care system.
Pourtant, c’est la dernière place où tu: Yet it’s the last place you should end up,” he says, hoping people can get care before it’s too late. He tells us how afraid his neighbours are of going to the hospital, because they fear they won’t be listened to or taken seriously. “Yet it’s obvious that people need care.” In the meantime, he does the work himself. “I want us to train residents so we have a citizen 911. We call our own people, at least we know what’s going on around us. If we don’t have that, here, nobody else will do it.”
À l’intérieur des murs de la SHAPEM se t: For 15 years, the offices of Paroles D’Exclues have been located inside SHAPEM’s walls. The nonprofit’s mission is to foster citizen mobilization. It is in their space that Manon and Daniel prepare the food. Neighbourhood residents can also come by to chat, have a coffee, get information, propose ideas.
« Il y a beaucoup d’écoute des besoins p: “There’s a lot of listening to needs to see whether measures can be taken and lead to change, just as there’s a lot of referral to resources,” explains Marie-Soleil Garzon, a mobilization officer.
Un immeuble de la Société d'habitation p: A building of the Société d'habitation populaire de l'Est de Montréal (SHAPEM), in Montréal-Nord. Photo: Christelle Saint-Julien
Comme l’organisme n’offre pas de service: Because the organization doesn’t provide services, its staff sometimes find themselves backed into a corner. “It’s something that could have not happened,” says Christine*, a former mobilization officer, of the three deaths she witnessed. Another occurred just before she started in the role. How many people have died alone on the island of Montréal? Impossible to say; no data is recorded on the subject. “I know four, and four is four too many,” Christine sums up sadly.
Dans ces circonstances, difficile de con: Under these circumstances, it is hard to know the scale of the phenomenon elsewhere. She is the one who found Marcel’s body after a neighbour told her she no longer heard him coming and going. “The neighbours had said Marcel wasn’t doing well,” she recalls. It was the same story for Célia. “How many times did we send her to the hospital before they found out she had a degenerative disease?” she asks.
Elle s’explique difficilement la mort d’: She struggles to make sense of Elzéar’s death. “We lost him, we shouldn’t have lost him. I fought for him to get home care, he was an elderly person. I had really put a red flag on his situation,” she says of the man who lived alone and had grown fond of her. He often called her to thank her. The man, who was in his sixties, had no family. “There are a lot of people in Montréal-Nord who are alone, who have no social network,” she points out. Neighbours noticed a smell and raised the alarm.
Les services d’urgence ont découvert sa: Emergency services found his body in his apartment. Christine is not a social worker; she compares her former role instead to that of a neighbourhood organizer. “At the very least, I can assess what the person needs,” she says. The mobilization officer takes steps with social services to obtain follow-up care. “I was knocking on doors and getting no answer, it was complicated,” she says.
Plusieurs citoyens n’osaient pas télépho: Many residents didn’t dare call 911 in an emergency; they called Christine first, sometimes on a Saturday at midnight. “I always answered the phone. I urged them to call 911, I told them what to say. ‘Yes, but they’re going to be mad at us,’ they’d answer. I told them no,” Christine illustrates; she has since left her position. She speaks to the toll these regrettable situations have taken on residents. “There are a lot of people living alone who see this and think, ‘That could happen to me.’ I could fall in my apartment, and nobody would notice. This loneliness is terrible.”
Sa collègue Marie-Soleil Garzon abonde d: Her colleague Marie-Soleil Garzon echoes her. “Guilt, helplessness, frustration,” she lists, describing residents’ feelings. “Residents created a social safety net for themselves because they saw that if they didn’t, they could lose people.”
Au Québec, c’est le Centre intégré unive: In Quebec, it is the integrated university health and social services centres (CIUSSS) that are tasked with helping the population get the health and social services it needs. CIUSSS are divided by sector and oversee, among other things, hospitals and local community service centres (CLSC). Marie-Hélène Giguère, head of the population relations and public relations service at the CIUSSS du Nord-de-l’Île-de-Montréal, says the government body is present in nonprofit housing for seniors – which SHAPEM is not, since it offers housing to all. The spokesperson says that the lack of access to services and the deaths of people alone in their homes have not been raised at the sector’s seniors’ roundtable, nor in any of the CIUSSS’s various programs and services.
« Après vérification auprès de notre équ: “After checking with our community organization and public health team, I can confirm that community mobilization around seniors is particularly dynamic in Montréal-Nord at the moment,” says Ms. Giguère. She notes that the outreach teams, who go door to door, can be counted on to prevent deconditioning among older people, as can close collaboration with community partners and the regional public health department. That is not what those working on the ground observe. Marie-Soleil Garzon believes residents are left to fend for themselves and forced to look after one another. “They try to fill the gap, but it’s not up to them to do it. It’s not their responsibility. They already have to take care of themselves and their daily burdens,” she says.
Elle demande qu’il y ait des services de: She is calling for community-based services that go out to people, since many have known health problems. “It takes proximity. Not everyone can afford to get to the CLSC, and it’s intimidating for someone who doesn’t feel confident,” she says. She believes the current system is designed for those who are able to travel to services, who have been treated well from the start or who don’t feel stigmatized. “Some people don’t have a phone to make an appointment, others don’t know how – it’s designed for a certain population, it remains inaccessible to everyone,” sums up Ms. Garzon.
Des expériences de santé de proximité on: Community-based health initiatives have been carried out with residents on occasion. Ms. Garzon would like a long-term project put in place, with people who act as a link, who get to know residents and who are ready to do interventions or consultations. “It’s a format that works well with residents, and it’s one of the ways that lets them open up and feel confident. It takes versatility, basically, and flexibility,” she believes. For example, in seniors’ residences there is staff on site, just as there is a nurse in a school. “Once you’ve found help, you also have to be able to keep it,” continues her former colleague Christine. “The CLSC works a lot on request.
Ces gens-là ne demandent plus », témoign: These people no longer ask,” she says. She suggests that street outreach workers, like those who work with youth, be sent to seniors. “It would be interesting to identify people who are alone, to assess their needs.” And, in the long term, follow-ups must also be provided consistently. She believes public health services need to do an about-face, and she hopes for better collaboration between them and community organizations. “What I can see is that workers want to do community outreach – get out of the CLSC, out of the hospital, and go into the field,” says Christine, who has met many practitioners. That willingness to act has to go in a certain direction. “Public health is a huge ocean liner, you can’t turn it around as you please.”
Si ces décès se sont produits dans des l: Although these deaths occurred in SHAPEM housing, Christine believes the nonprofit is doing what it can. We contacted SHAPEM about this, but had not received a response at the time of writing. “It is still an important player in social housing, one that is connected in its community,” says Marc-André Desrochers, the organization’s former director of territorial mobilization. He explains that the social housing nonprofit develops ties with community organizations and social services, but does not offer support as such to tenants. Housing people with different profiles creates all kinds of challenges for the organization. To get a unit, residents must apply through the Office municipal d’habitation de Montréal. He points out that social services lack resources, in particular front-line workers on the ground. “A nonprofit can’t afford front-line workers.
Ça ne peut pas faire partie d’une équipe: That can’t be part of a team in place in a community. It’s not the landlord’s role, fundamentally,” he says. Mr. Desrochers believes isolation is a societal problem, one that is less visible at SHAPEM than elsewhere. “Seniors, isolated people, they’re everywhere in our communities. But we see the capacity, and especially the will, to build connections, which means people are less alone than others,” he says with satisfaction. There is no point in pointing fingers for the deaths. “It may be that the person cut themselves off from their community for all kinds of reasons, over which they have control. All kinds of reasons can explain why a person is isolated.” In his view, many people don’t want visitors. So who helps people who are alone and vulnerable? To avoid the worst, resident Daniel Bissonnette hopes everyone will get into the habit of knowing their neighbours and the people around them. “We have to keep going, not stop, help. That’s the goal.”
